Pakistan will host a major International Hockey Federation (FIH) event after a gap of 24 years, with the fifth edition of the FIH Hockey Men’s Nations Cup scheduled to be held in Lahore from February 19 to 28, 2027.
FIH President Tayyab Ikram and interim Pakistan Hockey Federation (PHF) President Mohyuddin Ahmad Wani announced the decision at a ceremony in Islamabad on Friday, where they also formally signed an agreement for the hosting of the 10-team tournament.

Iraq’s crude oil production hit 4.6 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, the highest since 2019, data from the International Energy Agency’s monthly report showed on Friday, as OPEC’s second-largest producer hiked output by 540,000 bpd from September.
Kuwait and Saudi Arabia also boosted their October crude oil output compared to September, as rising volumes of oil are leaving the Strait of Hormuz on smaller tankers, which then transfer the crude cargoes onto supertankers in the Gulf of Oman.
Iraq’s October crude oil production topped its OPEC+ quota by about 170,000 bpd, showed the data in the IEA’s Oil Market Report for November.
Kuwait also boosted its crude oil production last month, from 1.58 million bpd in September to 2.03 million bpd in October, although the Gulf producer was still about 650,000 bpd short of its OPEC+ ceiling.

Nov 13 - Polish President Karol Nawrocki vetoed legislation on Friday that would have let regulators decide whether online content is illegal and order it blocked, his second rejection of a bill implementing the European Union’s Digital Services Act.
Nawrocki said the bill, which had been narrowed and resubmitted after he vetoed an earlier version in January, gave state officials excessive power over online speech.
"It is not the role of an official to rule on whether a given piece of content constitutes a crime or not. That is solely the role of independent courts," he said in a video on X.

text:
Egypt has revoked the citizenship of brothers Anas and Tarek Habib after they acquired foreign nationality without prior government approval, according to two Cabinet decisions published in the Official Gazette on Thursday, 12 November.
The decisions, signed by Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly, were issued on 1 and 2 November following a recommendation by the Minister of Interior and Cabinet approval.
Decision No. 90 of 2026 revoked the citizenship of Tarek Ibrahim Abdel-Rahman Habib, born in Beheira Governorate in September 1994, while Decision No. 93 applied to Anas Ibrahim Abdel-Rahman Mohamed Habib, born in Saudi Arabia in July 1998.
Under Egypt’s Nationality Law No. 26 of 1975, Egyptians are required to obtain permission from the Minister of Interior before acquiring another nationality. Those who do so without permission may have their Egyptian citizenship revoked through a Cabinet decision.
The decisions did not specify which foreign nationality either brother had acquired.

text:
The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.
After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.
Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.

text:
What's going on with the polar vortex?
November 13, 2026
High up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons. This is the polar vortex.
If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere.
Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.
Earliest vortex disruption on record
It's not yet clear how the current disruption to the polar vortex will affect the Northern Hemisphere winter, but scientists agree it is a record-breaking event.
"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told the AFP news agency.

Thien-Huong Ninh Villarreal, who teaches sociology, ethnic studies and business, has managed to hold two full-time and seven part-time jobs at different community colleges in the Golden State and made nearly $800,000 in 2024.

There are no rules limiting how many colleges or districts an instructor can work within and no tracking systems to monitor a professor's workload as each of California's 73 districts is governed independently.

A power plant built at the landfall of the Nord Stream gas pipelines in northeastern Germany was shut down after the pipelines were sabotaged. Now the facility is being dismantled and sent to Ukraine.
The Greifswald industrial power plant in Lubmin is majority owned by Germany’s Securing Energy for Europe (SEFE). Adrianne Montgobert, a spokesperson for the state-owned company, confirmed to RFE/RL that dismantling of the plant is currently under way, with its transfer being managed by a team from Naftogaz, Ukraine’s oil and gas giant.
The Nord Stream pipelines, which run under the Baltic Sea from Russia to Germany, are no longer operational.
The spokesperson said in an e-mail, “all reuse and sale options [for the Lubmin plant] were explored including actual sales negotiations, but no commercially viable solution emerged.” Donating the facility to Ukraine, Montgobert added, was seen as “the best alternative to scrapping it,” after it ceased operation in April 2023.

Koshary, the Egyptian dish of rice, pasta and black lentils topped with fried onions, was inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 10 December 2025, the first Egyptian food to be listed.
The listing covers more than a recipe. UNESCO’s entry describes a daily habit that feeds people across Egypt at low cost and gives work to cooks, street vendors, farmers and the craftspeople who build the carts it is sold from. Almost a year on, it is still the only dish among Egypt’s 11 entries on the UN cultural agency’s heritage lists.
What is koshary?
The UNESCO entry describes koshary as a filling, budget-friendly meal made from “simple, affordable ingredients”: rice, pasta, black lentils and fried onions. text:
Around 2020, Amy Terry noticed she didn't feel like her usual self.
The 50-year-old Michigander was working as a director of programming at a health association when she says she began experiencing symptoms like memory loss, low energy, mental processing difficulties — or, as she describes it, "waking up every day feeling like you were slogging through mud."
"I went from being this highly competent professional person to barely being able to get through phone calls," Terry says.
As the healthcare system strained under the weight of the Covid-19 pandemic, Terry, like many other people, struggled to get care. When she finally did, she found out it wasn't Covid-19. It was perimenopause.
Terry got through a few more years juggling her symptoms with her job, but by 2023, she couldn't hold out any longer. She quit to start independent consulting.

text:
BMW has recalled 720,796 vehicles in the US due to a fire risk and urged owners to park their cars outside, away from buildings and other vehicles, until repairs are completed, Reuters reported.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) issued the warning after identifying a potential electrical fault involving the vehicles' water pumps. The affected cars had previously been recalled in 2024 over a water pump issue but now require further repairs.
According to the report, an improperly sealed electrical connector on the water pump could be exposed to water, potentially causing a short circuit and increasing the risk of fire, even when the vehicle is parked and switched off.
BMW is still working on a fix for the latest recall and has reported 10 fire incidents that may be linked to the issue. These incidents occurred after the vehicles had already undergone repairs under the 2024 recall, the report said.

The large studios of Abdul Rahman Katanani and Ayman Baalbaki are filled with canvases and installations about memory and destruction, drawn from the Israeli wars that shaped both artists’ youth.
These magical spaces, one in an anonymous building in busy central Beirut, and the other far from the city in a village high in the hills, speak for Lebanon and Palestine.
They also define the two artists and their families.
Katanani’s materials are barbed wire, corrugated metal sheets, olive branches, petroleum barrels and discarded clothes from his birthplace, the Sabra and Shatila refugee camp.
“I’ve always wanted to use the materials of the camp. These materials are our shadows. No... they’re us,” he told Middle East Eye.

text:
The government is considering stripping back legal protections that limit the costs community groups face when challenging planning decisions that threaten nature.
The Aarhus convention, an environmental treaty that was signed into law by the UK in 2005, guarantees the legal right to participate in democratic processes on environmental matters – such as sewage pollution, new roads or datacentre developments.
Under the treaty, when an individual brings an environmental legal claim, they are protected by a cost cap that means they pay only £5,000 of the other side’s costs if they lose. For organisations, the cost cap protection is £10,000.
The purpose of this is to ensure legal challenges about the environment are not prohibitively expensive for individuals and public interest groups.

text:
Senior Chabad rabbi condones killing Jewish politicians who work with Arabs
A senior Chabad rabbi has been criticised by his own movement after he said it was permissible to kill Jewish Israeli politicians who worked with Arabs.
Gedalia Axelrod, a senior cleric in the Chabad-Lubavitch Hasidic movement, issued a halakhic ruling earlier this week in which he said that Jewish politicians who form a government backed by Palestinian citizens of Israel were "din rodef", which roughly translates as "law of the pursuer".
Under Jewish religious law, a rodef is someone who poses a threat to another person's life and may be stopped by any means necessary.
The doctrine was previously invoked by Yitzhak Rabin’s assassin, Yigal Amir, to justify the prime minister’s killing in 1995.
Axelrod wrote that collaboration with Arab parties "poses a terrible danger to the people of Israel in the Holy Land and around the world".

Under the new rules, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) will be allowed to respond to cyberattacks by foreign powers with counterattacks of its own. text:
OpenAI on Friday announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its "dots" artificial intelligence agents to make purchases on behalf of users.
The company built ChatGPT Wallet in partnership with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, and it allows cardholders to maintain their existing credit card rewards and protections. Eligible users enter their card information once, prompt their dot to find items to buy and approve each purchase with a security check.
OpenAI said its dots agents will never actually access a user's card details. Instead, their payment networks will provide the dot with a "payment token," which contains a scoped card number, security code and expiration date that is specific to a given transaction.
"Our goal here is to really focus on merchants and our network partners and start building out a really great foundation that's safe and easy to use," Chaya Nayak, who leads product for monetization and payments at OpenAI, told CNBC in an interview.

text:
The UK’s largest insurer has been hit by a rise in subsidence claims after an extremely hot summer left households across the country grappling with the fallout from the growing climate crisis.
Aviva said on Friday it had experienced the jump amid an industry-wide surge in households filing subsidence claims with their insurers to cover repairs, which typically are needed to address cracks, sloping floors, and off-kilter doors and windows.
It follows two record hot summers in the UK; August this year was the joint hottest month ever recorded around the world. Drier summers cause the ground under houses to shrink, which undermines a property’s foundations. It then expands in wetter winters, which can further damage homes.
Aviva experienced a “peak subsidence period” between July and September, with claims continuing into October, its chief executive, Amanda Blanc, told Bloomberg in an interview on Friday. Aviva would not provide any further detail on the scale of the increase in claims.
ai_summary: Aviva reported a surge in subsidence insurance claims in the UK following record-breaking hot summers.

text:
The world’s oil supply is swinging back to a surplus for the first time since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, the International Energy Agency (IEA) has said.
Oil supplies outstripped demand by almost 2m barrels a day in October, the Paris-based agency said, as “Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand”.
The market was “showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran”, the IEA reported.
It comes after months of disruption to the global oil market as the Middle East conflict blocked shipments via the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply normally passes.
The conflict has triggered a rise in energy prices this year. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, traded at about $72 a barrel in February, before the conflict began, and hit $126 a barrel by the end of April.

A prominent rabbi in Israel has invoked a Jewish religious doctrine permitting the use of lethal force against politicians who cooperate with Arab parties, Haaretz reported.
Rabbi Gedalya Axelrod, a former head of the Haifa Rabbinical Court, said in a handwritten ruling that Jewish party leaders who support a government formed with the backing of Arab parties are subject to din rodef, or the “law of the pursuer”.
Axelrod wrote that collaboration with Arab parties "poses a terrible danger to the people of Israel in the Holy Land and around the world".
Under Jewish religious law, a rodef is someone who poses a threat to another person's life and may be stopped by any means necessary. The doctrine was invoked by Yitzhak Rabin’s assassin, Yigal Amir, to justify the prime minister’s killing in 1995.

Crude inventories rose by 1.7 million barrels per day in October as exports from the Gulf recovered faster than worldwide demand, the Paris-based IEA said in its monthly market report on Friday.
Inventories climbed by 2.3 million bpd to 105.4 million bpd last month, raising output by an "extraordinary" 5.3 million bpd since August, the IEA said. Gulf oil exports, excluding Oman, hit 18.4 million bpd in October, which was 26 per cent below prewar levels as attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz continued.
That narrowed the year-on-year output decline to 2.9 million bpd, compared with an average loss of eight million bpd loss from March to September, the agency added.

Israel extends $3,500 departure grant to nationals of all African countries
Israel is extending its $3,500 voluntary departure grant to nationals of every African country in a bid to reverse a decline in the number of migrants leaving with state assistance, according to Haaretz.
Until now the payment had been limited mainly to people from a handful of states.
The change took effect on Monday and will remain in place until the end of the year, Israel's Population and Immigration Authority said. Applications must be submitted by 31 December.
It covers African nationals who have stayed in Israel for more than two years without a valid visa, and those holding temporary residency permits.
For the first time, it also includes people who entered Israel legally but overstayed their visas.

title: Russian Oil Discounts Hit 3-Year High as Middle East Supplies Recover
summary: Analysts said rising supplies from Persian Gulf producers were increasing competition for Urals.
text:
Russia’s flagship Urals crude was offered at its steepest discounts to Brent in more than three years in early November as Middle Eastern supplies recovered and India cut purchases of Russian oil.
Urals was offered at a $31-per-barrel discount to Brent at Russia’s Baltic ports and a $33 discount at the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk between Nov. 1 and 6, according to Argus data cited by the Kommersant newspaper. Both discounts were the widest since April 2023.
Argus attributed the widening to weak demand and high shipping costs.
Export volumes held steady despite the wider discounts. Shipments from Baltic ports averaged about 1.5 million barrels per day, in line with early October levels, while exports from Novorossiysk were little changed at 762,000 barrels per day.
India’s crude imports through the Strait of Hormuz rose to 2.1 million barrels per day in November, surpassing the 1.8 million barrels per day it imported from Russia, according to data from shipping analytics firm Kpler.
ai_summary: Russian Urals crude oil discounts reached a three-year high due to recovering Middle Eastern supplies and reduced demand from India.

title: IEA downgrades outlook on global oil demand growth, projects decline by 2.7 mbd in 2026
summary: According to the International Energy Agency, oil consumption growth will move into positive territory starting around March 2027
text:
MOSCOW, November 13. /TASS/. Global oil demand will decline by 2.7 mln barrels per day (mbd) in 2026, International Energy Agency (IEA) reported.
Thus, the agency has lowered its demand forecast by nearly 100,000 barrels per day (bpd) compared to its October expectations when a decline of 2.6 mbd was expected.
At the same time, the IEA expects the fall of global oil demand to slow to 2.7 mbd in the fourth quarter of this year from 4.4 mbd in the second and third quarters, reflecting a partial normalization in the supply of petroleum products, according to the report.
Oil consumption growth will move into positive territory starting around March 2027, which will drive an increase in demand of 2 mbd in 2027, the agency said.
According to the IEA’s forecast, global oil demand will reach 102.285 mbd in 2026, compared to 104.969 mbd in 2025. For 2027, the agency expects oil demand at 104.297 mbd.
ai_summary: The IEA has downgraded its global oil demand outlook, projecting a decline of 2.7 million barrels per day for 2026.

text:
An estimated 1.1 million people died from tuberculosis worldwide in 2025, despite a 35 per cent decline in deaths from the disease over the past decade, the World Health Organisation has said.
The WHO disclosed this in its 2026 Global Tuberculosis Report, released on Thursday, noting that TB remained “the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent” globally.
According to the report, “an estimated 10.6 million people developed TB, and 1.1 million people died from TB” in 2025, while treatment had saved an estimated 86 million lives since 2000.
The organisation said the decline in deaths meant the world had reached the first mortality milestone of its End TB Strategy, although “five years later than planned”.
It, however, warned that progress in reducing new infections remained slow, with the global TB incidence rate declining by only 14 per cent between 2015 and 2025, against the 50 per cent reduction target set for 2025.

title: Russian oil exports up to 6.82 mbd in October, revenues up to $21.15 bln
summary: Revenues from exports increased by $3.61 bln month-on-month to $21.15 bln due to growth of oil prices
text:
MOSCOW, November 13. /TASS/. Russia’s exports of oil and petroleum products rose by 260,000 barrels per day (bpd) in October 2026 to 6.82 mln barrels per day (mbd), the International Energy Agency (IEA) reported.
Revenues from exports increased by $3.61 bln month-on-month to $21.15 bln due to growth of prices for oil. This is the highest level since this May.
Oil deliveries from Russia were flat at 5.33 mbd in October, while supplies of petroleum products went up by 260,000 bpd to 1.49 mbd. Revenues from oil exports totaled $17.22 bln last month, which is $2.53 bln higher than in September, while revenues from exports of petroleum products amounted to $3.93 bln (up by $1.08 bln compared with September).
Moreover, the price of Russian Urals FOB Primorsk grew by $6.98 to $101.28 per barrel, the report said.
Compared to October 2025, Russia’s revenue from oil exports in October 2026 was $8.33 bln higher.
ai_summary: Russian oil and petroleum product export revenues rose to $21.15 billion in October 2026, driven by increased export volumes and higher prices.

Azzi on the Beat doesn’t exactly ease listeners into Mara Gram. On its opening track Police Way, sirens blare, drums clatter and another rhythm seems to barge in before the first has finished. This is mara, the fast, sample-heavy dance music that grew out of carnivals and neighbourhood parties in working-class Lagos, with tempos reaching 160 beats per minute.
Born Waris Rasheed, Azzi on the Beat grew up in the Lagos neighbourhood of Bariga, where he joined a free after-school arts academy at five and trained as a traditional dancer before becoming a producer. Now aged 22, he makes beats live on stage, often dancing and performing acrobatics as he goes. His breakout track Mr Barry has racked up millions of streams, while his debut album Mara Gram makes an intriguing case for the sound’s possibilities.

When critics of colonialism decry legacy institutions of British rule seldom do they bring up the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The JCPC is largely unknown to the general public, but decades after decolonisation it continues to serve as the final appellate court for Britain’s overseas territories, Crown Dependencies and roughly a dozen Commonwealth nations.
In those countries which have opted to remain under its jurisdiction, citizens can appeal the judgments of their highest domestic courts to the London-based panel. As a result, members of the JCPC are among the only English jurists to still hear death-penalty cases.
The JCPC’s latest judgment does not involve the death penalty, but a matter which is even more inflammatory in many former colonies. Hungary (261 mln euro), Bulgaria (230 mln euro), and Greece (166 mln euro) take the lead in natural gas purchases. Slovakia purchased gas from Russia worth 127 mln euro.

Egypt has broken new ground in international digital trade, becoming the first country outside Europe to achieve full technical alignment with the European Union’s electronic signature and seal framework.
The milestone was cemented through a new administrative arrangement signed between Egypt’s Information Technology Industry Development Agency (ITIDA) and the European Commission.
By placing Egypt onto the EU’s Advanced Electronic Signatures (AdES) Trust List, the deal eliminates traditional cross-border paperwork bottlenecks, allowing Egyptian and European companies and government bodies to verify digital contracts, stamps, and official documents seamlessly across borders.
Why Egypt’s edge matters
A historic first: Out of every non-European nation worldwide, Egypt is the very first to pass the EU’s rigorous technical evaluation for electronic trust interoperability—positioning Cairo as a premier digital bridge between Europe, the Middle East, and Africa.

A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.
All that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.
The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

summary: Researchers found that dementia risk increases with the number of cigarettes smoked per day, rising by 16% for those who smoke 10 a day and by 34% for those who smoke 20, compared with people who have never smoked.
text:
Researchers found that dementia risk increases with the number of cigarettes smoked per day, rising by 16% for those who smoke 10 a day and by 34% for those who smoke 20, compared with people who have never smoked.
A scientific review involving about 2.8 million people found that smoking is associated with an increased risk of dementia, Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia, with the risk rising as the number of cigarettes smoked per day increases.
According to the study, which was led by researchers from Curtin University in Australia and published in the journal "eClinicalMedicine", smokers face a 31% higher risk of developing dementia compared with people who have never smoked.

title: Belift Lab loses damages suit against ex-ADOR CEO over alleged defamation
summary: SEOUL, Nov. 13 (Yonhap) -- A Seoul court on Friday ruled against K-pop agency Be...
text:
Belift Lab loses damages suit against ex-ADOR CEO over alleged defamation
SEOUL, Nov. 13 (Yonhap) -- A Seoul court on Friday ruled against K-pop agency Belift Lab in a suit claiming damages from Min Hee-jin, former CEO of K-pop label ADOR, for alleged defamation.
Belift Lab, a sub-label of K-pop powerhouse Hybe, had sought 2 billion won (US$1.5 million) in damages after Min claimed in an April 2024 press conference that the label's girl group Illit had copied ADOR's NewJeans.
The Seoul Western District Court rejected Belift Lab's argument that Min had defamed the label by spreading false information, ruling her remarks were an expression of subjective opinion.
It also dismissed a counter suit raised by Min against Belift Lab, seeking 5 billion won in damages.
 Min faces a separate criminal case over the alleged defamation against Belift Lab, with police referring her to the prosecution last month on suspicion of defamation and obstruction of business.
 yunhwanchae@yna.co.kr
(END)
ai_summary: A Seoul court ruled against K-pop agency Belift Lab in a defamation lawsuit against former ADOR CEO Min Hee-jin, citing her remarks as subjective opinion.

Countries have gathered at the annual climate change negotiations at the COP31 summit in Turkey to discuss how to achieve a goal that is increasingly unachievable. On the misty Tilarán Mountain Range above Monteverde in Costa Rica, a rare combination of circumstances has led to something special.
A pocket of forest constantly shrouded in thick cloud supports an enormous variety of specialist plants and animals. For many of them, this is the only place on Earth they are found.

Some 400 bird species live here, from the spectacularly loud three-wattled bellbird to the long-tailed manakin, famed for its males' courtship dance. title: Japan team creates ‘planimal’ hybrid plant-animal cells in world first
summary: Cells that produce useful animal and plant proteins and can be cultured using photosynthesis could offer new methods of producing drugs and meat.
text:
A Japanese team said that it has become the first in the world to create hybrid plant-animal cells, dubbed “planimal” cells, by fusing a unicellular alga called Cyanidioschyzon merolae into cultured animal cells.
According to the team from the University of Tokyo, the Institute of Science Tokyo, Kindai University and others, all of C. merolae’s DNA was integrated into the animal cells’ chromosomes.
But the hybrid cells were, in terms of function, animal cells because C. merolae’s DNA was suppressed and chloroplasts, which conduct photosynthesis, were degraded during fusion.
“We hope to introduce chloroplasts and activate C. merolae genes to generate oxygen through photosynthesis,” said Sachihiro Matsunaga, professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Frontier Sciences.
The team’s findings were published in the international journal Nature Communications.
Matsunaga had been working on the production of planimal cells since he proposed the creation of such a hybrid in 2018.
ai_summary: Japanese researchers have successfully created hybrid plant-animal cells by integrating algal DNA into animal cells, marking a world-first in biotechnology.

text:
Daya Thussu was still a student when he landed a subediting desk job at the Press Trust of India (PTI), then India’s largest news agency.
It was the early 1980s, and the newsroom in New Delhi was alive with the clatter of telex machines delivering dispatches from across the world.
At his desk, Thussu, then in his mid-20s, worked through two very different streams of international news. One came from established Western agencies, including Reuters. The other arrived through a little-known network connecting newsrooms across Asia, Africa and Latin America.
“We would check the ticker to see what the story was and where it had come from,” Thussu says of his work with the Non-Aligned News Agencies Pool (NANAP). “It could be from anywhere - the Philippines, Iraq or across Africa. My job was to select stories that we would then send out to the PTI wires.”

title: Who gets to tell the world’s news?
summary: A look back at the Global South's early efforts to challenge Western dominance of international news.
text:
Daya Thussu was still a student when he landed a subediting desk job at the Press Trust of India (PTI), then India’s largest news agency.
It was the early 1980s, and the newsroom in New Delhi was alive with the clatter of telex machines delivering dispatches from across the world.
At his desk, Thussu, then in his mid-20s, worked through two very different streams of international news. One came from established Western agencies, including Reuters. The other arrived through a little-known network connecting newsrooms across Asia, Africa and Latin America.
“We would check the ticker to see what the story was and where it had come from,” Thussu says of his work with the Non-Aligned News Agencies Pool (NANAP). “It could be from anywhere - the Philippines, Iraq or across Africa. My job was to select stories that we would then send out to the PTI wires.”

title: Treasury yields rise as traders strengthen Fed rate hike bets

Treasury yields edged higher on Friday as investor expectations for a December rate hike by the Federal Reserve gathered strength.
The 10-year U.S. Treasury note yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose 2 basis points to 5.1271%.
The longer-dated 30-year Treasury bond yield, which tends to react to geopolitical risks, was 3 basis points higher at 5.4602%. The 2-year Treasury note yield, which is typically more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was 1 basis point lower at 4.8525%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
The upward moves come after 10-year Treasury yields jumped more than 13 basis points to more than 5% during Thursday's session, and the 2-year yield soared more than 15 basis points.

Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm in 12 hours. Lisbon saw 183 flights cancelled on Wednesday, around a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.
After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. title: What truly makes a workplace great? By Olubukola Lanipekun-Lawal

text:
A company can invest millions in its modern offices, offer competitive salaries and provide attractive employee benefits, yet still fail the people whose work sustains it. The warning signs may not appear on a balance sheet immediately. They emerge when talented employees stop contributing ideas, when capable people leave because they see no future, and when teams become more concerned with avoiding blame than achieving meaningful results.
A great workplace is not defined solely by what an organisation provides on paper. It is revealed by how people experience work every day, and by what they are able to accomplish because of it. Their judgement, creativity, commitment and ability to work together shape the quality of decisions, the strength of customer relationships and the institution’s capacity to adapt. Workplace culture is therefore not a soft consideration. It is a strategic asset that drives organizational performance, resilience and long term sustainability.

title: Torture chambers exist in nearly every Ukrainian city — Russian security source
summary: Non-residential premises and basements are often used for this purpose
text:
LUGANSK, November 13. /TASS/. Torture chambers exist in nearly every city in Ukraine, and their number is difficult to determine, a source in Russia’s security services told TASS, noting that basements are often used for this purpose.
"It is impossible to say exactly how many torture chambers there are in Ukraine. They exist in virtually every city and in every regional capital. Non-residential premises and basements are often used, so outsiders have no way of seeing what goes on. The instruments of torture can vary widely, depending on the imagination and cruelty of those who use them," the source said.
He added that Ukrainian nationalists continue to hold people unlawfully despite media coverage of the torture chambers.
ai_summary: A Russian security source claims that torture chambers are present in nearly every Ukrainian city, utilizing basements and non-residential premises.

title: Toyota Tsusho to participate in 900 MW wind farm project in Egypt

text:
Toyota Tsusho will participate in an independent power producer (IPP) project to develop, own and operate a 900 MW wind farm in Egypt. The project will be undertaken through Aeolus, a joint venture between Toyota Tsusho group company Eurus Energy and France-based CFAO.
The project will be developed by Shokeir Wind Energy, a local company funded by Aeolus, France-based Engie and Egyptian engineering and construction company Orascom Construction. The wind farm, Gulf of Suez Wind Farm III, will be located in the Gulf of El Zayt area along the Gulf of Suez. It will comprise 86 wind turbines, each with a capacity of 10.5 MW.
Trial operation of the first 300 MW is scheduled to begin in January 2028, followed by phased capacity additions. Full commercial operation is expected to start in September 2028.
Electricity generated by the wind farm will be sold to the Egyptian Electricity Transmission Company under a 25-year power purchase agreement.

LOS ANGELES - How do journalists report on a war when they become victims of the violence, and when their proximity to the conflict is used to paint them as unreliable witnesses?

title: China stages unannounced Pacific drills in ‘silent intimidation’ push: Taiwan officials
summary: Beijing has stepped up its military pressure over the past five years, drawing condemnation from Taiwan and heightening concern in the West.
text:
TAIPEI – China carried out a large, unannounced military exercise across the western Pacific and around Taiwan in early November, in what officials in Taipei have described as a campaign of “silent intimidation” aimed at pressuring Taiwan and other governments before major international meetings.
A senior Taiwan security official, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, said China’s military and coast guard had at one point massed more than 100 vessels in the region early this month, conducting drills that included simulated attacks on other militaries and cities including Taiwan’s.
The naval deployment was larger than “Justice Mission 2025,“ China’s last formally named drills targeting Taiwan nearly a year ago and one of the largest Chinese naval deployments to date, the official said.
ai_summary: China conducted large, unannounced military exercises near Taiwan, involving over 100 vessels in a move described by Taipei as silent intimidation.

text:
طقس معتدل نهارًا وبارد ليلًا بشمال سيناء.. شبورة مائية وفرص لسقوط أمطار خفيفة
يسود مدن محافظة شمال سيناء، اليوم، طقس خريفي معتدل الحرارة نهارًا، مائل للبرودة ليلًا وفي الساعات المتأخرة من الليل والصباح الباكر، مع ظهور شبورة مائية صباحية على عدد من الطرق، ونشاط للرياح الخفيفة، وسط توقعات بسقوط أمطار خفيفة على بعض المناطق.
وأوضحت الهيئة العامة للأرصاد الجوية أن درجات الحرارة بمدن محافظة شمال سيناء تتراوح ما بين 7 و26 درجة مئوية، حيث تسجل مدينة العريش درجة حرارة تتراوح بين 12 و26 درجة، ومدينة رفح بين 11 و25 درجة، بينما تتراوح درجات الحرارة في مدينتي الحسنة ونخل بوسط سيناء بين 7 و23 درجة مئوية.
وأشارت الهيئة إلى تكون شبورة مائية على مختلف مدن المحافظة، خاصة مناطق وسط سيناء، مع وجود فرص لسقوط أمطار خفيفة، ونشاط للرياح الخفيفة على أغلب الأنحاء.
وفي السياق ذاته، تواصل غرفة العمليات الرئيسية بمحافظة شمال سيناء متابعة تطورات الأحوال الجوية، بالتنسيق مع غرف العمليات الفرعية بمجالس المدن والمديريات المعنية، مؤكدة استقرار الحالة الجوية، وعدم تلقي أي إخطارات أو شكاوى تتعلق بالظروف الجوية حتى الآن.

title: Aeolus reaches financial close for Egypt’s 900MW wind farm project
summary: Aeolus reaches financial close for Egypt’s 900MW wind farm project Yahoo Finance
text:
AEOLUS, a Toyota Tsusho Group company, has announced the financial close of the Gulf of Suez Wind Farm III project in Egypt, a development set to add 900MW of wind power capacity to the country's grid.
The wind farm will be constructed in the Gulf of El Zayt area along the Gulf of Suez, furthering Egypt's renewable energy initiatives.
The project will be developed by Shokeir Wind Energy, a joint venture comprising AEOLUS, which holds a 40% stake, ENGIE with 35%, and Orascom Construction with the remaining 25%.
The wind farm will use 86 turbines, each with a capacity of 10.5MW.
This development represents AEOLUS' third wind investment in Egypt.
Power generated from Gulf of Suez Wind Farm III will be sold to the Egyptian Electricity Transmission Company under a 25-year power purchase agreement (PPA).
According to the project timeline, commissioning of the initial 300MW is expected to begin in January 2028, with the entire facility scheduled for full commercial operation by September 2028
ai_summary: Aeolus has reached financial close for a 900MW wind farm project in Egypt's Gulf of Suez, scheduled for completion by 2028.

وزير الصحة يبحث مع مسؤول سنغافوري تعزيز التعاون الصحي ودعم المنظومة المصرية
استقبل الدكتور خالد عبدالغفار، وزير الصحة والسكان، ذو القرنين عبدالرحيم، الوزير المسؤول عن الشؤون الإسلامية ووزير الدولة الأول لشؤون الدفاع بسنغافورة، لبحث سبل تعزيز التعاون الثنائي في القطاع الصحي وتطوير أطر الدعم الإنساني والطبي المقدم للمرضى والمصابين جراء الأزمات في قطاع غزة والسودان.
رحب الوزير بالوفد السنغافوري، مؤكدًا عمق العلاقات التاريخية بين البلدين والشراكة الاستراتيجية المتميزة في المجالين الصحي والإنساني. وتناول اللقاء آليات تفعيل بنود مذكرة التفاهم الموقعة بين وزارتي الصحة في البلدين خلال زيارة رئيس جمهورية سنغافورة للقاهرة في سبتمبر 2025، والتي تشمل مجالات الرعاية الصحية الأولية والأمراض غير السارية والتحول الرقمي وسلاسل الإمداد الطبي.
وأكد الجانبان ضرورة تشكيل لجنة توجيهية مشتركة لمتابعة تنفيذ خطط العمل وتعزيز برامج تبادل الخبرات والزيارات بين الأطباء والفرق الطبية في التخصصات الدقيقة، وخاصة برامج التدريب الطبي المستمر ونموذج «تدريب المدربين» في تخصصات الغسيل الكلوي للأطفال وجراحات القلب والأورا

text:
The Dutch government is in crisis after a proposed "millionaires’ tax" exposed such deep divisions that the three-party coalition is at risk of crumbling after less than nine months.
Parties bickered over a deal with the left-wing opposition to support a 2027 tax plan in exchange for an increase of wealth taxes. The conservative People’s Party (VVD), the third group in the governing coalition, threatened to quit if the measure passed.

title: After suffering its worst election result, what's next for the ANC — and for South Africa?
summary: A crushing local election result across the country has left South Africa's ruling ANC searching for answers. Experts say the vote reflects public frustration with service delivery failures — signaling a political shift.
text:
ANC election collapse: A new political era in South Africa?
November 13, 2026
South Africa's governing African National Congress (ANC) party is forced to confront its worst electoral setback to date after securing under 31% of the vote in the country's significant local government elections; party leaders themselves have described the result as "catastrophic."
This outcome marks a steep decline for the party that had once led South Africa's liberation struggle; the party that had dominated the country's political landscape since the end of apartheid in 1994.
The result reflects growing public frustration about the ANC's lack of performance in key areas such as skyrocketing unemployment, poor service delivery, local governance failures and years of graft and corruption — sometimes at the highest levels of government.
So what comes next for the ANC — and for South Africa?
Voters express growing frustration and despair

India’s capital, Delhi, overtook Lahore to become the world’s most polluted city on Friday, with air quality reaching hazardous levels and visibility dropping as smog blanketed the city of 20 million people.
Earlier, Delhi’s air quality index (AQI) stood at 334, categorised as “hazardous”, making it the most polluted major city globally, according to Swiss air quality monitoring group IQAir, which measures pollution levels based on the concentration of pollutants. An AQI reading of up to 50 is considered good, indicating little or no health risk.
India’s official Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), meanwhile, recorded a higher AQI of 403 in Delhi and classified the air quality as “severe”.
The difference between the Swiss and Indian readings is due to the different AQI scales and methodologies used to calculate and classify air pollution levels.

title: Mohammed Kazem on four decades of pushing the boundaries of Emirati art
text:
Hail pellets broke through the awning. They pierced holes in the corrugated green plastic. Sunlight streamed through the holes the following morning, casting facsimile shapes of light in the shade. To the young Mohammed Kazem, the holes looked like eyes. They were on the blinds, in the shadows on the walls and on the ground, enveloping him from above, from below. The eyes changed as the day progressed. They grimaced. They frowned. They squinted as if mid-laugh. The setting and its interconnected state had taken on an anthropomorphic quality. Light and shadow had put on faces.
This was in the winter of 1996. Kazem was in the house of his mentor, the late artist Hassan Sharif. He commented on the faces he saw in the damage and Sharif brought out his camera, encouraging him to capture what he was seeing. Kazem began taking photographs of the awning and its shade. The close-ups resembled portraits. The series was titled Faces to Face. It was exhibited at the Sharjah Art Museum in 1998.

Russian troops have pushed units of the Ukrainian armed forces 30 km away from the Russian state border in the Kursk Region to the Yunakovka settlement in the Sumy Region, making the broadest section of the buffer zone in the area, military expert Andrey Marochko told TASS.
"If we're talking about where the broadest buffer zone in the Sumy Region is, it’s the Yunakovka sector--this is exactly where our guys advanced the furthest after crossing the state border and driving Ukrainian militants out of Sudzha. text:
A Montana-born photographer who spent much of his adult life in Seattle has left behind an unusual legacy, 480 acres of farmland worth an estimated $1 million, now earmarked to support Alzheimer's research in his hometown. According to an announcement by the Weissman Hood Institute, Arnold Swanberg, who died in October 2024, bequeathed two parcels of agricultural land to the research institute in Great Falls, Montana. In 2026, the donation is drawing attention for the role it could play in advancing research into Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and other neurodegenerative diseases.

There has been a backlash in many Western countries against the arrival of irregular migrants fleeing conflict, authoritarian rule and economic hardship in their home countries.
Legal humanitarian migration dropped “sharply” by 26pc in 2025 compared with 2024, the report found. Labour migration increased by 13pc.

title: Africa: Wp235 - Law Ahead of Opinion? Abortion Law and Public Morality in 38 African Countries
summary: [Afrobarometer] Where the law has gone furthest, it has moved well ahead of what the public morally accepts.
text:
Where the law has gone furthest, it has moved well ahead of what the public morally accepts.
Abstract
Abortion law has been relaxed faster in Africa than anywhere else since 2000, but whether opinion has moved with it was unknowable before Afrobarometer's Round 10 surveys of 2024/2025, which asked 50,961 people in 38 countries whether abortion can be justified in four circumstances. Opinion depends on the circumstance. Acceptance averages 66% when the woman's health or life is in danger, 51% after rape or incest, 33% under economic hardship, and 29% for any reason. Religious affiliation does not predict opinion. Age, urban residence, schooling, and how common people believe abortion to be around them are stronger predictors. Law and opinion are only loosely connected. ai_summary: A study across 38 African countries reveals a complex, loose connection between the liberalization of abortion laws and public moral acceptance.

The Guards said the strike was in retaliation for what they described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in Iran's southern Sirik county, in Hormozgan province, according to Iranian state media.
The claim came amid a fragile lull in the conflict between Iran and the US, which began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28 and has since spread across the region.
Iran launched missile and drone attacks on US bases in Gulf states and sought to restrict shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global oil and gas supplies. Washington, in turn, imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.

title: Sudan: Does Your Culture Shape How You Look At Art? What an Eye-Tracking Study in Sudan Revealed
summary: [The Conversation Africa] Today, Old Dongola is an abandoned settlement on the banks of the Nile in northern Sudan. Hundreds of years ago, however, this place looked very different.
text:
Today, Old Dongola is an abandoned settlement on the banks of the Nile in northern Sudan. Hundreds of years ago, however, this place looked very different.
During the Middle Ages, Old Dongola was the capital of the Kingdom of Makuria, which adopted Christianity in the 6th century. Nearly 700 years after the fall of the kingdom, many medieval buildings have survived beneath the desert, including the remains of churches and monasteries. Their walls still preserve paintings, of archangels or biblical scenes or local rulers and dignitaries.
There have been several studies of these paintings to learn about the religious life, politics and art of medieval Nubians. But, as a team of psychologists, cognitive scientists, archaeologists and heritage managers from European and Sudanese institutions, we decided to ask a different question: how does the culture we come from influence the way we look at them?

text:
UNRWA funding cuts deepen hardship for Palestinian refugees in Lebanon
Funding cuts and Israel’s war have left Palestinians in Lebanon in increasingly dire circumstances.
Beirut, Lebanon – Doumoua al-Baitan sat on the roof of a building in Beirut’s Palestinian refugee camp of Bourj el-Barajneh as the sun set. Like many Palestinian refugees in Lebanon, al-Baitan was born and raised in this camp.
For decades, Palestinians in Lebanon have been supported by the UN branch focused on Palestinian refugees, UNRWA. But funding cuts have impeded UNRWA’s ability to provide crucial aid, particularly since the Trump administration’s decision in February 2025 to maintain a US funding freeze imposed the previous year.
Between the funding cuts and funding shortfalls, UNRWA has had to close down or reduce hours of schools, healthcare centres, and clinics in Lebanon’s Palestinian refugee camps.

ai_summary: Funding cuts and the ongoing conflict have severely restricted UNRWA's ability to provide essential healthcare and education to Palestinian refugees in Lebanon.

LAHORE: The Lahore High Court has ruled that consumer courts lack jurisdiction to entertain complaints filed by policyholders against insurance companies.
Justice Jawad Hassan issued the ruling on a petition filed by the United Insurance Company of Pakistan Limited against an order passed by the District Consumer Court in Bhakkar.
The consumer court had overruled an objection raised by the insurance firm regarding the maintainability of a complaint filed by a policyholder.
The district court had held that the complaint was maintainable simply because the dispute stemmed from the provision of insurance services.
Setting aside the consumer court’s order, Justice Hassan observed that the lower forum failed to properly examine the relevant statutory framework, specifically Section 122 of the Insurance Ordinance, 2000.

However, for farmers to maximize these benefits, preserving diverse habitats and effectively managing tree growth to ensure adequate light for cacao trees is essential.
text:
Nature has mysterious ways of sustaining itself without any human interference. Due to our increasing demand, we have evolved mechanisms such as fertilisers, pesticides and even modifications in seeds to improve yields and get a better harvest. However, time and again, we find that nature also keeps evolving as per its requirements, which can make the lives of farmers who depend on it easier. In Peru's Amazon region, researchers have found that wildlife on farms, such as bats and birds, could be worth thousands of dollars to cacao growers.
A study of 28 organic cacao agroforests in the northern Peruvian Amazon found that birds and bats help control crop-damaging pests, contributing to almost twice the cacao yield in landscapes rich in trees. The researchers estimated that this natural pest-control service could add around US$1,640 per hectare annually in production value. Indonesia’s fiercest fires in at least a decade were amplified by an “El Niño that turned off the taps” and “fossil fuels that turned up the heat”, scientists have revealed.
Along with the conversion of forests to plantations, this created the conditions for blazes that have burned almost 3m hectares (7.4m acres) – 19 times the size of Greater London – this year, and cast a choking haze across much of south-east Asia.
An international team of World Weather Attribution scientists analysed the different elements of this triple whammy in Java, Kalimantan and Sumatra to assess how each affected the peak fire season from August to October.
They found global heating, primarily driven by the burning of oil, gas and coal, raised temperatures by 1.6C in this three-month period, drying the land and vegetation.
On top of this, El Niño, which is on course to break all records, added a further 0.3C and reduced rainfall by about 50%.

title: El Nino, climate change supercharged Indonesia fires, study says
summary: Indonesia's worst fire season in years cloaked local towns and neighboring countries such as Singapore and Malaysia in toxic smog.
text:
A strong El Nino and human-induced climate change fueled the hot and dry weather over Indonesia this year that sparked the country’s worst wildfire season in a decade, according to new research.
El Nino was the driver of the severe lack of rainfall, while climate change was the cause of high temperatures, a report by World Weather Attribution shows. Human-induced warming made hot and dry conditions about three times more likely, as well as more intense, researchers said.
Indonesia’s worst fire season in years cloaked local towns and neighboring countries such as Singapore and Malaysia in toxic smog, prompting schools to close, straining diplomatic ties and crimping palm oil output. Poor rainfall from June through the end of October left the landscape bone-dry, making blazes often linked to slash-and-burn agricultural practices harder to contain.

SEOUL, Nov. 13 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's rice output declined for the fifth consecutive year in 2026 amid changing dietary habits, data showed Friday, with the cultivation area also reaching a new low.
Rice production decreased 0.9 percent on-year to 3.5 million tons this year, according to data compiled by the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
It marked the fourth-lowest level since the government began compiling the data in 1965.

Despite the decline in overall production, output per 1,000 square meters increased 0.2 percent on-year to 524 kilograms this year, according to the ministry.

SEOUL, Nov. 13 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's money supply continued to rise in September from a month earlier, driven by increases in short-term deposits and money trusts, central bank data showed Friday.
The country's M2, a key gauge of the money supply, stood at an average of 4,283.9 trillion won (US$3.2 trillion) in September, up 0.4 percent, or 17.1 trillion won, from a month earlier, according to preliminary data from the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The figure has risen steadily since November last year.
The M2 is a measure of the money supply that includes cash, demand deposits and other easily convertible financial instruments.
The BOK said short-term deposits and money trusts with maturities of less than two years increased in September.

MOSCOW/DUBLIN – Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed on Thursday that European representatives could join the next round of Ukraine peace talks, a U.S. envoy said, though the Russian leader said Washington must work with its European allies to understand if they want peace or war in Ukraine.
The move to give Europe a seat at the negotiating table at the next round of talks, announced by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, could mark a breakthrough. But Putin’s comments underlined how difficult the negotiations could become, given sharp differences between Moscow and European capitals over the way the war should end.

text:
Outgoing Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, a Republican, acknowledged Thursday that the Lone Star State "turned purple" after Democrats' so-called blue wave swept statewide races and flipped the governor’s office, a U.S. Senate seat and Texas House.
During his latest episode of the "Lt. Dan Podcast," Patrick acknowledged that Texas’ political makeup is shifting left but stopped short of saying the state had turned blue after many others had described it as now a blue state.
"Right now, I’d say it’s purple," he said. "We've been winning consistently, and people see it as a red state. But this time, the Democrats turned out more of their Democrat voters than Republicans turned out of their voters. But what really made the difference were the independent voters, the voters who don't vote in Republican or Democrat primaries. They only vote in general elections.
"For almost every election, we’ve been winning those voters. We didn’t win them now. Will they stay voting for Democrats in the future?

text:
Nigeria’s merchandise exports to China fell by N601.82bn in the second quarter of 2026, despite Beijing’s decision to grant Nigerian products zero-tariff access to its market from 1 May, worsening the trade imbalance between the two countries.
An analysis of the National Bureau of Statistics’ foreign trade reports for Q2 of 2025 and 2026 showed that Nigeria’s exports to China declined by 54.30 per cent, from N1.108tn to N506.57bn.
The decline occurred even as Nigeria’s imports from China increased by N955.58bn, or 19.26 per cent, from N4.96tn to N5.92tn during the same period.
Consequently, Nigeria’s merchandise trade deficit with China widened by N1.56tn, or 40.43 per cent, from N3.85tn in Q2 of 2025 to N5.41tn in the corresponding period of 2026.

At about 7:30 p.m., the boat was halfway across the Eleyele River when its engine died.
For a few seconds, there was only the sound of water against the plastic hull. Then the wind began to rise. Passengers shifted uneasily on the wooden planks. I looked towards the far bank—close enough to see, yet suddenly too far.
The operator did not panic. He reassured us and tried the engine again; it wouldn’t work, so we waited. Minutes later, another boat appeared and towed us to safety.

AMSTERDAM: International students are turning away from the United States and Britain in favour of universities in Asia and continental Europe, a global university survey showed on Thursday, as tighter visa rules redraw the global map of higher education.
International students typically pay far higher fees than domestic ones and are a major source of revenue, helping offset their host countries’ teaching and research costs.
Britain and the US recorded the steepest drops in international undergraduate numbers, down 19pc and 13pc, respectively in the October-August period compared with the same period a year earlier, the survey of 437 universities in 63 countries conducted by Studyportals, NAFSA and Oxford Test of English showed.

A widespread outage hit Microsoft platforms including Outlook on Thursday, with many users encountering trouble using their email accounts and other errors across the tech giant's suite of apps.
Nearly 130,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook just after 1 p.m. ET. New reports have since fallen from that peak, but many said they couldn't send and receive emails or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether.
Thousands also reported issues with Microsoft's workplace messaging app Teams, as well as its AI assistant Copilot and wider Microsoft 365 services.
Microsoft said it was investigating disruptions, notably related to its email and Teams applications.

Foreign government officials often remark, with genuine puzzlement, that Japanese bureaucrats must never sleep. When a major announcement comes out of the United States in the morning, European counterparts have until close of business to begin formulating their response. Japan, by rights, should be asleep, yet its ministries are still awake, scrambling to keep up in real time. Two of Europe's rarest chicks are thriving at Chester Zoo after keepers used an improvised hot-water bottle made from a rubber glove to help them survive.
The two Malay peacock-pheasant chicks are the only known members of the endangered species to have hatched in a European zoo this year.
According to the European Association of Zoos and Aquaria (EAZA), just 15 Malay peacock-pheasants are recorded in European zoos.
As few as 2,500 are thought to remain in the wild, where extensive habitat loss has pushed the species towards extinction.
Bird keepers at the Cheshire zoo stepped in when the chicks' mother failed to sit on her first egg.
Recognising the importance of every hatchling, they transferred the egg to a bronze-tailed peacock-pheasant, a closely related species, to be incubated.

text:
Nearly two months after ICE agents whisked a beloved California nurse and professor from her home in Lodi, her university has ramped up calls for her release.
“She needs to come home,” said Eileen Fry-Bowers, dean for the University of San Francisco’s nursing school,in reference to Ann Lawani, who was arrested by immigration agents in September and has since been shuffled between detention centers in California, Texas, and Louisiana, in a series of opaque transfers.
Lawani, 39, came to the US in 2007. She established herself as a nursing professional, obtaining a master’s and doctoral degree in the field, before stepping into academia.
She steers two programs at the University of San Francisco, one a master’s entry program geared toward students with non-nursing backgrounds and another a bachelor’s program for students seeking to work in public health safety-net institutions.
“She basically has her hands on almost 300 students that she engages with on a regular basis,” Fry-Bowers said.

text:
It has been kept secret for decades, buried four metres deep into the white cliffs of Dover. But from Friday, members of the public will finally be able to visit a pioneering command bunker that was ordered by Winston Churchill and proved a vital defence during the second world war.
The Fan Bay plotting room, which is encased in concrete, housed the first land-based computer-aided targeting system. This acted as a “brain” for a gun battery that was used to defend Dover and attack German ships in the Channel, according to Jon Stewart, who led the excavation project for the National Trust.
Stewart was the first person to enter the bunker when it was rediscovered in 2017 after it had been secretly mothballed in 1957 and classified until 1981 owing to its military importance.
“It was a Tutankhamun moment for a conflict archaeologist,” he said. “We had done all this research on the people who had served there, and then suddenly you’re standing in their office. It was an exciting moment.”

title: An endangered leatherback turtle tried to nest on an Ecuador sidewalk before finding a quieter beach
summary: Bella, a resilient leatherback turtle, made a remarkable nesting attempt in Ecuador, overcoming an array of challenges posed by artificial lighting. Her successful hatchling rates reveal a promising trend, indicating that leatherbacks are beginning to adapt to their new coastal environments. Conservation efforts are increasingly vital as these turtles face persistent threats, highlighting the urgent need to establish safe habitats for their upcoming nesting seasons.
text:
In January, under the light of a full moon and one too many streetlights, a critically endangered leatherback turtle named Bella did something both remarkable and worrying: she tried to nest on a sidewalk in Ecuador.
Disoriented by nearby streetlights, the enormous female crawled over a rock breakwater and left the beach behind. She failed to lay her eggs there and returned to the ocean, still carrying them. Two nights later, she tried again, this time on a quieter stretch of sand at Playa de Crucita. There, she dug a nest, deposited 47 eggs, covered them carefully, and returned to the sea.
A few weeks later, 44 hatchlings emerged and made their way toward the surf. Bella, it turned out, was only beginning. Researchers who had tagged her during her first attempt found that she nested four or five times during the 2026 season. Across all her nests, 146 eggs produced 134 hatchlings, i.e. a 91.8% success rate.

title: Without Jensen Huang, Nvidia's organizational structure isn't 'built to last,' management expert says
summary: Nvidia's flat management structure could pose challenges for Huang's successor, according to experts.
text:
Jensen Huang resigned Thursday as CEO of Nvidia, the chipmaking company he co-founded in 1993, following public revelations of his extramarital affairs. Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, will serve as the company's interim CEO.
Huang's visionary leadership style and his central role in driving the company's strategy, combined with the company's unusually flat management structure, will make him especially difficult to replace, experts say.
Huang notably had more direct reports than the typical CEO, with a "direct staff" of approximately 60 employees, he said in a March 2026 interview with podcaster Lex Fridman.
"The more direct reports a CEO has, the less layers are in the company. It allows us to keep information fluid," Huang told CNBC's Andrew Ross Sorkin in 2023.

ai_summary: Management experts suggest Nvidia's flat organizational structure may struggle following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang.

St Cloud Officers responded to a stalled vehicle blocking traffic in the 1300 block of 13th Street North around 7.49pm Wednesday.

Pro-Palestinian group seeks ban on Israeli real estate fair in Paris
Pro-Palestinian activists have asked a French court to ban an Israeli real estate fair in Paris marketing Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, AFP reported on Thursday.
The Franco-Palestinian NIDAL association filed an emergency motion with a court against the 9th Icube real estate and investment salon, arguing that the fair violates human rights.
The event is scheduled for Sunday at the European Centre for Judaism in the French capital. Other major cities have seen similar uproars over Israeli real estate fairs.
NIDAL asked the court to either order the head of the Paris police force to ban the event outright or to ensure that the event does not sell property in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, whose occupation by Israel since 1967 is considered illegal under international law.

Wetzel leaps backward as the mother approaches him, then Congdon reaches over the fence and grabs Wetzel's shirt, trying to pull him forward.

title: Skyrocketing regional airfares hurting patients needing specialist care
summary: Residents and medical professionals say WA's reliance on FIFO doctors leaves regional residents vulnerable to rising flight prices.
text:
Skyrocketing regional airfares hurting patients needing specialist care
In short:
Medical services in regional WA are directly impacted by high airfares.
Local practices say flight costs are hurting their ability to attract doctors and provide care.
What's next?
The Productivity Commission is due to release its final report on regional airfares next year.
Residents and medical professionals say Western Australia's increasing reliance on fly-in,fly-out doctors for specialist care leaves country patients heavily exposed to skyrocketing regional airfares.
An interim report from the Productivity Commission released this week found regional Australians are paying excessive fares to travel within their own state.
The commission found short regional flights were on average 173 per cent more expensive per kilometre than major routes.
The same flights, often only provided by one operator, are used by medical specialists to visit regional areas across WA.

title: British veteran returns to an Argentine veteran the helmet he took in 1982
summary: A former Royal Marine has travelled to Argentina to return to an Argentine veteran the helmet he took during the Battle of Mount Harriet in the 1982 Falklands War, in a reunion filmed for a documentary, BBC Sussex reported.
text:
A former Royal Marine has travelled to Argentina to return to an Argentine veteran the helmet he took during the Battle of Mount Harriet in the 1982 Falklands War, in a reunion filmed for a documentary, BBC Sussex reported.
Andy Gatrick, who was 18 at the time of the war, came across two injured Argentine soldiers during the Battle of Mount Harriet, fought on June 11 and 12, 1982. Both were captured by the Marines. Gatrick kept the helmet of one of them, which bore a name: Hector. Now 63, he managed to track him down and on October 23 flew to Gualeguaychú, in Entre Ríos province, to return it in person to Héctor Pereyra.
“I put my weapon down and as I bent down to put the strap over my shoulders, I saw movement and a cloth which looked like a white handkerchief. My eyes adjusted and there was two Argentinians, I didn’t know they were badly injured. I dived to the floor, weapon up.
